The White-browed antbird (Myrmoborus leucophrys) exhibits a distinctly altricial developmental strategy, with neonates emerging from the calcareous egg at a remarkably early stage. This relatively brief egg stage yields a hatchling with minimal feathering and limited motor capacity, reflecting a pattern common among many suboscine passerines. The wet weight of these newly hatched chicks is approximately 2.6 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.6 grams], a mass that is modest even by antbird standards and underscores the substantial post-hatching developmental trajectory that lies ahead. The energetic demands of this rapid growth phase are met through intensive biparental provisioning, with both adults delivering arthropod prey to the nestling at frequent intervals. This early life history strategy, characterized by a short incubation window and a small neonatal mass, appears to be an adaptation to the high predation pressure typical of Neotropical forest understories, where prolonged nest exposure carries considerable risk.

The combination of a low daily mortality risk and a gradual reproductive pace aligns with a classic slow life-history syndrome, typical of many tropical forest birds that experience relatively stable environmental conditions and high adult survival. The confluence of these traits—moderate clutch size, delayed first reproduction, extended lifespan, and a modest metabolic rate—positions the White-browed antbird as a representative example of the life-history strategies that have evolved in the competitive and stable environments of Neotropical rainforests.
